chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
title: Stravinsky's telegram and the Ebony Concerto premiere at Carnegie Hall
summary: Herman describes receiving a telegram from Stravinsky, who wrote a piece for the band; it was premiered at Carnegie Hall in 1946 and recorded in California.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: I think that was probably the most thrilling -- it was, undoubtedly, that ever happened in my musical career and life. To receive a telegram from Igor Stravinsky, saying that he had heard some of our music and he

was now writing a piece -- he was writing a piece for the Woody Herman band. And this -- I received this, I think, probably along about October, this telegram. And he said, "I hope to have the piece completed and will come to New York and bring it in time for Christmas to you -- to the men in the band and you."

And, imagine having something like this happen to someone in my position or the guys, and, well, I flipped out and so did the guys in the band. It was all arranged through a mutual friend who actually became some way or other a music publisher, but not as a publisher but as a song plugger for a publisher. But he was a very astute guy, and he was a former bassist, he'd been in a couple of bands. And somehow, he got to latch on to Mr. Stravinsky and he started to play our records for Mr. Stravinsky. Then I believe that somewhere along the line he decided that he was going to write a piece for this group of mad young people.

And eventually, he did bring it to New York and it was presented to us, and we -- he rehearsed it and taught it to us, actually, because we weren't that accomplished, to play pure Stravinsky, because that's what it was. It wasn't jazz, nor was it meant to be. As he put it, the challenge was to write for with such bastard instrumentation, and he did add, -- he said, because he had to add a horn and a harp.

And -- but basically, it was his music, as it should have been. And we learned to play the music, and presented it at Carnegie Hall in 1946, at our first jazz concert. And the critique was quite broad, some of it with great gusto and enjoyment and some of it couldn't understand what it was about and so consequently I would say it would remind me of some of the things that still happen.

however, And, all in all, we took the thing on the road then and [played ] it every night, and did a concert tour. Then, when we got to the Coast, Mr. Stravinsky was now home, and he lived not far from here (inau- where we're sitting. dible). And we decided we would record it, and do an album or whatever you would call them in those days.
I think so, yes, an album. And he said, "I would never cut my music, but," he said, "I will for you."
